candidates.text: The envelope was addressed to me in my own handwriting — my thirty-year-old handwriting, with the old loop on the *g* I'd long since abandoned — and the postmark read HALLOWAY, a village that had been a bus depot for forty years until the road was rerouted and the whole place folded back into a field. Inside was a single ticket, card stock gone the color of weak tea, torn from a spiral pad on a bus that had not run since the eighties. Route 44. Fare 40p. And there, crisp as ink from this morning, the date: tomorrow, the 14th, with the departure time struck in the ticket machine's uneven blocky type — 06:14. I had told no one I was going. I had told no one anything. But the seat number was the same one I took every morning for six years, riding out to the hospital where my mother worked the early shift, and the thought of sitting down there again made the back of my neck cold in a way the weather had nothing to do with. So at 6:13 the next morning I was standing on the corner with my coat buttoned to the throat, holding a ticket I had no intention of using, and when the engine turned over at the end of the street — a sound like the world remembering how to breathe — it was a green single-decker with the number 44 in the window, and the driver's face was the face of the man I buried in 1997.

instruction: Answer the brief, but make it creative.

task.brief: A bus ticket bought thirty years ago arrives in the post, dated tomorrow. Write the next paragraph.
good_idea_qualities: the ticket forces a small concrete decision
the paragraph makes the elapsed thirty years felt without explaining them
the ending leaves the reader uneasy rather than resolved
task.reference_text: The envelope had been forwarded twice and the postmark was this morning's. Inside, the ticket was warm, as though it had been held, and the destination printed on it was the town she had left at nineteen without telling anyone she was going.
